tfn.s: Hudson's new word, minning, means doing something less, or not at all.
tfn.why: The text says: “you do it less, or not at all.”

tfn.why: The text says the opposite: “Health, sleep, friendships and habits are not tasks you complete.”

tfn.s: Dictionary.com compared August 2026 with a 2025 monthly average to show how fast maxxing was growing.
tfn.why: The text says: “by August 2026 the term was appearing in digital media 19 times as often as its monthly average in 2025.”

tfn.s: Kelly Wright believes maxxing will disappear because middle-aged people have adopted it.
tfn.why: The text says she suspects it will stay: “that usually kills the cool without killing the word.”

tfn.s: Polly Hudson has stopped using maxxing words in her own life.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text describes her column but not her own habits.

tfn.s: Donnelly's concern is that the language treats parts of life as things that can be completed.

tfn.s: The text suggests the minning column was based on research into how many people have given up self-improvement.
tfn.why: The text says: “Minning is one writer's joke, not a trend anybody has measured.”

speak.title: Role-play: maxxing or minning?
speak.setup: Work in pairs. Read your card, then have the conversation. Swap roles and do it again.

a.text: You love tracking your sleep, food and steps. You want your friend to join a 30-day plan with you. Explain what you enjoy about it, and listen to your friend's worries.

b.text: You're tired of scores and targets. You want a weekend with no apps and no plans. Say why, and ask your friend to try it with you.

phrases: I've been tracking my sleep for a month.
That's too much like homework for me.
I'd rather do less, not more.
Don't you feel better when you can see the numbers?
We could try a plan that's half and half.
I'm not sure that's fair, but I'll try it.
speak.after: Afterwards, tell the class: did you agree on a plan, and who changed their mind?
